_comment: SHARED FIXTURE - identical bytes in all four frameworks.
tina4-python/tests/fixtures/batch_write_contract.json
tina4-php/tests/fixtures/batch_write_contract.json
tina4-ruby/spec/fixtures/batch_write_contract.json
tina4-nodejs/test/fixtures/batch_write_contract.json
BATCH WRITES COST ONE ROUND-TRIP PER ROW. Feature 3 of the feature audit.
All four frameworks loop execute() once per row inside executeMany:
python  for params in rows:            self.execute(sql, params)
php     foreach ($paramsList as $p)    $this->execute($sql, $p)
ruby    params_list.each { |params|    drv.execute(sql, params) }
node    for (const params of sets)     await adapterExecute(...)
Identical shape, identical defect. On a networked engine that is N round
trips for N rows, and the round-trip IS the cost of the write - not SQL
building, not placeholder conversion. MEASURED, 500 rows, .99 host, from a
macOS workstation (PHP 8.5.7):
engine        row-at-a-time      one multi-row VALUES     speedup
PostgreSQL         9848 ms                   15.8 ms        625x
MySQL              4816 ms                   22.3 ms        216x
MSSQL              2594 ms                   21.4 ms        121x
SQLite (WAL)          1.3 ms                  0.4 ms        3.5x
A 500-row seed costs TEN SECONDS on PostgreSQL and should cost sixteen
milliseconds. FakeData::seedTable/seedOrm and any bulk import pay this.
THE COLLAPSE LIVES ABOVE THE ADAPTER. A multi-row VALUES list is SQL
building, which adapter_contract.json deliberately keeps off the adapter
(executeMany is on its not_on_the_adapter list). One implementation per
framework in the SQL translator - the unit all four already have above the
adapter - instead of the same edit in six Python, ten PHP, seven Ruby and
seven Node adapters, which is exactly the 4.3x this row exists to remove.
No mocks. The speedups above are re-measured against live engines by each
framework's runner; the pure chunking rules below are checked without one.

function._note: Same concept, same name, idiomatic casing. A PURE function: SQL + parameter sets + engine name in, a list of (sql, params) statements out. It performs no I/O, so its rules are checkable without a database - the live engines then prove the speedup is real.
function.returns: A list of [sql, params] statements to run in place of the row-at-a-time loop. An EMPTY list means 'not collapsible - keep looping', which is always correct and is the required fallback for every case the rules below do not accept.

max_bind_params._note: The hard per-statement bind-parameter ceiling of each engine. Chunk size is derived from it, never guessed: chunk_rows = max(1, floor(cap / columns)). Exceeding a cap is a runtime error on a real engine, so these are conservative floors, not aspirations.
max_bind_params._zero_means: 0 = DO NOT COLLAPSE. ODBC's ceiling depends on the driver behind it and cannot be assumed; MongoDB is not SQL; Firebird is its own case, below. All three keep the row-at-a-time loop.
_firebird: VERIFIED against live Firebird 5.0.4 on the .99 host, not assumed:
INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (?, ?), (?, ?)          -> rejected, -104 Token unknown
INSERT INTO t (a, b) SELECT ?, ? FROM RDB$DATABASE  -> rejected, -804 Data type unknown
So Firebird genuinely has no multi-row VALUES, and SQL rewriting is correctly ruled out here.

BUT THAT IS NOT THE WHOLE ANSWER, AND THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS NOTE WAS WRONG. It concluded Firebird could only be batched by a form that knows each column's TYPE (CAST(? AS INTEGER) per column, or EXECUTE BLOCK) and therefore needed schema introspection. That looked only at SQL syntax and never at how the DRIVER is used.
Measured against live Firebird 5.0.4, 300 rows, no SQL change of any kind:
A. a new cursor per row (what the adapters do today)   3128 ms
B. ONE cursor, reused across the batch                 1489 ms   2.1x
C. the driver's own executemany()                      1729 ms   1.8x
D. an explicit prepared statement, executed N times    1677 ms   1.9x
The adapters call conn.cursor() inside every execute(), so every row pays a fresh PREPARE. Reusing one cursor for the batch halves the time with no CAST, no EXECUTE BLOCK and no column types.

So Firebird stays at cap 0 - it must never emit multi-row VALUES - and gets its win from statement reuse instead. That is an adapter concern (how a driver is driven), not a SQL-building one, which is exactly why it does not belong in build_batch_inserts and why cap 0 is the right entry here.
Firebird remains the slowest engine on this path even after the 2.1x, at roughly 5ms per row against 0.07ms for a collapsed PostgreSQL batch.
max_bind_params._why_sqlite_999: SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER is 999 before SQLite 3.32 and 32766 after. 999 is the safe floor and still collapses 333 three-column rows into one statement. MEASURED, 5000 rows: chunk=1 5.56ms, chunk=333 (this cap) 1.99ms, chunk=10922 (a 32766 cap) 2.02ms. The conservative floor costs NOTHING - it already captures the whole win - so raising it would only add risk on pre-3.32 builds.
max_bind_params._why_mssql_2100: SQL Server's absolute parameter limit per statement is 2100. It is by far the tightest cap here, which is why chunking is mandatory rather than an optimisation.

_note: The four frameworks DO NOT agree on what an engine calls itself, so the cap lookup must normalise before it reads the table above. Measured 2026-07-30:

This is real drift and it is exactly the kind a shared fixture exists to catch: without normalising, the collapse silently does nothing on PostgreSQL in two of the four frameworks - the engine with the largest measured win. It was caught here by a live run showing PostgreSQL still taking 10.2s while MySQL and MSSQL had dropped to milliseconds.

Normalising here is deliberate and narrow. Renaming what the adapters report would be a breaking contract change touching migration, ORM DDL and dialect dispatch in all four; that belongs in its own row of the audit, not smuggled into an optimisation.

collapsible._note: EVERY condition must hold. Anything else returns empty and loops - a batch that silently writes the wrong rows is far worse than a slow one.
conditions: the statement is a single-row INSERT INTO <table> (<cols>) VALUES (<placeholders>)
its VALUES list contains ONLY positional placeholders - no literals, no expressions, no nested function calls
there are at least 2 parameter sets
every parameter set has the same length, and that length equals the placeholder count
the engine's max_bind_params is greater than 0
the derived chunk size is at least 2 rows

rejected._note: Each of these MUST return empty (loop). They are listed so every framework rejects the same things for the same reasons.
rejected.RETURNING: the caller expects one row back per statement; a collapsed statement returns N and would misreport last_id
rejected.ON CONFLICT: PostgreSQL upsert - conflict arbitration differs once rows are batched together in one statement
rejected.ON DUPLICATE KEY: the MySQL spelling of the same hazard
rejected.not_an_insert: UPDATE/DELETE/DDL have no multi-row VALUES form
rejected.literal_in_values: INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (?, now()) - repeating a non-placeholder per row is not a parameter substitution
rejected.ragged_params: parameter sets of differing length cannot share one column list
rejected.single_row: one row is already one round-trip; collapsing buys nothing

semantics._note: The collapse is an OPTIMISATION and must be invisible. These four properties are what the runners assert against live engines, because a faster batch that changes behaviour is a bug.
semantics.affected_rows: unchanged - the TOTAL number of rows written, not the number of statements run
semantics.last_id: unchanged - the id of the LAST row inserted
semantics.atomicity: unchanged - the whole batch stays inside one transaction on one pinned connection, and one bad row still rolls back every row, including rows in already-executed chunks
semantics.ordering: unchanged - rows are written in the order supplied, and chunk boundaries never reorder them

live_engine_cases.name: a_bad_row_rolls_back_the_whole_batch_including_earlier_chunks
live_engine_cases._note: Sharpest case. With MSSQL's 2100-parameter cap a 1000-row batch spans MULTIPLE statements, so the failing row lands in a LATER chunk than rows already executed. If chunk 1 survives a failure in chunk 2 the batch is no longer atomic and this optimisation has broken the write path.
